items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: Louis Armstrong. He was my idol... after I heard Louis Armstrong play, I had no doubts that I wanted to try to be a trumpet player.

ctx.x: Yesterday, when you were young — it sounds like a song — when you were growing up was there certain influences that led you to the trumpet?

Yes. Louis Armstrong. He was my idol. I was born in Kentucky and moved to Columbus, Ohio when I was six months old, so I didn’t know too much about Kentucky. I went back when I was five and stayed with my grandparents there for about seven years, whom he taught, my uncle taught me the scales on the trumpet, but he was never a schooled professionally, he just picked music up. So he taught me the scales. And I’ve tried to play ever since. I didn’t want to play, but after I heard Louis Armstrong play, I had no…
When you say you heard him, was there records in your house?

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I had no doubt in my mind I was going to try and be a trumpet player... And he’s still my idol. I think that Louis Armstrong was the greatest trumpet player ever lived.

ctx.x: How did he get his musical interest? Where did that come from? Seems he would be so occupied with making a living on the farm, that….did he work professionally?

He was a coal miner. And everyone there was a coal miner. And he used to listen to records. I think Bessie Smith was the most popular one there. And Mamie Smith. And I got interested in one that Louis Armstrong made with Bessie Smith. He made quite a few I think, him and Earl Hines and Coleman Hawkins. And that attracted my attention, and I began to listen to Louis Armstrong and from then on after I heard him play on these records I had no doubt in my mind I was going to try and be a trumpet player. I still am.…

they had some that worked on the radio and they had a symphony band around Columbus, OH-­ no blacks--so they were saying it’s impossible to play that high. And, the night of the performance he was in the Palace Theatre downtown and I got to go backstage and they said he had a trick trumpet, he had put chewing gum in the little hole in the mouthpiece. They used to do that, they’d make a smaller hole with the chewing gum so that would make them play higher. But they looked at his mouthpiece, it was just like you…

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: And he's been my idol every since. Ever since I first heard him play behind Bessie Smith.

ctx.x: Oh, yes, yes. All the old records of the old blues singers like Bessie Smith, Blind Lemon Jefferson. Oh, all the old Blues singers we had the records of. Then I happened to hear Louis Armstrong backing up Bessie Smith. And that's when it all started. That's for me. That's the direction I wanted to go in.
So that was when I was about 11 years old, you know. And he's been my idol every since. Ever since I first heard him play behind Bessie Smith. And I think Earl Hines was playing piano.
